p: This page replaces the Roadmap on the parent page (Mobile development assessment). It lists every step of Mobile plans 01 to 13 in the order we will do them. Each step has a row for its Jira ticket and its pull request (PR).

Why the order changed. The old roadmap grouped work by topic: quick wins, architecture, platform. The new one groups work by risk to customers. The customer app has many users. It ships every week. Old app versions stay on phones for months. So each step must reach customers in a way that cannot break the app, and that we can undo quickly.

li.p: Build the safety net first. Tests, release tooling, dashboards and the kill switch come before any change to app behaviour (Phases 0 and 1).
Change one risky thing per release. A release carries at most one flagged change or one approved delta. If something goes wrong, we know which change caused it.
Every risky change has a fast way back. A switch flag that turns the new path off in minutes, or a halted store rollout.
Each phase is one Jira epic. Put the epic key next to "Jira epic" under the phase heading.
Each row is one Jira ticket. Put the ticket key in the "Jira ticket" column.
Put the PR link (or links) in the "PR" column when the PR is opened.
"Plan ref" points to the plan page and step, for example "01 §0" = Mobile plan 01: Security, step 0. The details of each step stay on that plan page.
A phase starts only when the previous phase's exit gate is met. Rows inside a phase can run in parallel unless the row says otherwise.

Every step has one class. The class tells you how the step can affect customers and how to undo it.

Behaviour is meant to change. Product or the data protection officer signs it off first. Where possible, it has its own kill-switch flag.
Turn the kill switch off, or halt the rollout and hotfix.
The backend must change too. It must keep working for old app versions until the minimum supported version is raised.

li.p: One risky change per release. A release carries at most one class C or class D change. Class A and B changes can ride along.
Two dials, one at a time. The Play staged rollout and a switch-flag rollout are separate dials. Move only one of them in the same week.
Staged store rollout. Play: 5% → 20% → 50% → 100%. iOS: App Store phased release. Before each step up, check the release health dashboard.

Stop rules. Halt or flip back when the new version or the new path is worse than the old one by more than the agreed thresholds. Starting proposal (Mobile plan 04, step 8): crash-free sessions more than 0.2 points lower, error rate more than 10% higher, p75 screen load more than 10% slower, funnel conversion more than 2 points lower.
Backend changes go monitor-only first. A class E step logs what it would block, without blocking. It enforces only after the oldest supported app version can handle it.
The parity net must be green before a release. Unit and widget tests, golden screenshots, recorded API fixtures, the analytics golden names file, and the e2e journeys in automation-monorepo.

Old app versions are not affected by switch flags. A flag only exists in builds that contain the new path. Old builds keep their old code. This is why class C is safe for the long tail of old versions.

li.p: Who decides. The feature owner named in the flag catalogue decides each step up. The mobile on-call can flip back without asking.

p.strong: What moved compared with the old roadmap.

li.p: Coverage gate, one Flutter version and the analytics golden file moved earlier, into Phase 1, because they cost customers nothing and protect everything after them.
The analytics wrapper is split. The seams ship first with no change (Phase 2). The personal-data fixes ship later, one per release (Phase 3). Call sites move last (Phase 5).
dio interceptors moved out of the architecture phase into their own phase behind one switch flag (Phase 4). The refresh race touches every logged-in user.
The Riverpod 3 upgrade has its own phase (Phase 6), because it touches every screen.
The design-system package moved from "platform" to Phase 8, because the loan package needs it.
The e2e suite moved from "platform" to Phase 1. It is part of the safety net.
RASP is split: RFP now (Phase 1), SIT trial in Phase 3, prod in report-only mode first (Phase 10).
Owner. Who owns the roadmap and each epic? The Customer Mobile Apps squad with a named tech lead is the suggestion (parent page, question 1).
Stop thresholds. Product and SRE agree the numbers in "Release rules" before Phase 1 ends.
Minimum supported app version. Who decides when to raise it, and how often? Class E steps (3.10, 4.4, 4.8) need an answer.
Go or no-go at each rollout stage. Is it the feature owner alone, or the feature owner plus QA?
Coverage threshold. 70% on changed files to start (parent page, question 3).
RASP vendor and budget (parent page, question 2).
Design system: build our own or adopt DK's library (parent page, question 5). Phase 8 assumes we build our own.
